title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based lessons for training novice human tutors who teach middle school mathematics online. The focus is on lesson creation rather than student learning outcomes: the authors investigate how different levels of prompt decomposition affect the quality of generated lessons, and how LLM-generated lessons compare with human-crafted lessons.

The intervention/approach combines retrieval-augmented generation with GPT-4o. The authors used retrieved research articles on tutoring practices to prompt the model to generate structured lessons in English, each following a five-part format: title page, scenario 1, instruction, scenario 2, and conclusion. They tested one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-segment prompting strategies, where later segments were conditioned on earlier generated content.

The setting is online tutor professional development for novice tutors in middle school mathematics, with lesson quality evaluated by two experienced human coders and compared against lessons written by two human instructional designers. The paper finds that the three-segment strategy produced the best overall lesson ratings, outperforming single-step generation and slightly outperforming more highly decomposed approaches. Human reviewers saw clear benefits in time savings, diverse scenario generation, and generally appropriate content, but also noted weaknesses such as generic feedback, unclear writing in some sections, and unreliable references. The authors conclude that LLMs can support lesson drafting in a human-AI workflow, but human review remains necessary for quality, clarity, and citation accuracy.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical qualitative/benchmarking study of generated lesson quality, but it does not test learning outcomes and relies on human ratings and expert reflections rather than a controlled causal design. The evidence is informative for content generation quality, but it meets only limited credibility criteria for efficacy claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear promise for reducing authoring time and improving scalable lesson production, but it does not demonstrate measurable effects on student learning. Reported impacts are practical and workflow-oriented rather than direct educational gains.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4o with retrieval-augmented generation and prompt decomposition to automatically generate interactive, scenario-based tutor training lessons for novice tutors teaching middle school mathematics online

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that LLM-generated lessons substantially reduced lesson-drafting burden, especially for scenario sections and multiple-choice question creation. Two human lesson designers judged the system as time-saving and useful for creating reusable lesson drafts; however, no quantitative productivity effect size was reported (n=2 evaluators).
finding.measure: Human designer questionnaire / qualitative review of authoring workload and time-saving potential

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that hybrid human-AI workflows could help scale tutor-training content production, potentially expanding access to lesson development for middle school math tutoring programs. This is based on qualitative judgments from two designers and human ratings of generated lessons; no learner outcome data or institutional effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Expert judgments about scalability, reusability, and collaboration potential
